title: Hartwell Labs POC - weekly velocity & baseline compare
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latest latency/throughput bench results vs Hartwell's incumbent (NimbusServe). Redwood showed improved median latency with slightly higher tail under peak concurrency. Discussed routing playbook, KV cache warm-up, quantization options for cost tradeoffs, and next steps to run a 24h tail test and share an annotated benchmark spreadsheet.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-21
Start: 11:34 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lina (CSM), Jordan (Hartwell VP ML), Priya (Hartwell SRE), Tomasz (Lead Eng), Ana (Sec Ops), Benji (intern)

Auto-summary: weekly POC check-in, bench compare vs NimbusServe, routing and tail behaviour discussed

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining on short notice. quick readout from our side — we ran the throughput sweep yesterday and pulled p50/p95/p99 across the same request set you sent.
[00:18] Jordan: cool, thanks. we were really interested in the tail behaviour under sustained 300-400 conc.
[00:26] Ethan: right, so headline numbers — median for Redwood Dedicated at 256 tokens is about 140ms, p95 ~ 320ms, p99 ~ 610ms. NimbusServe numbers from your baseline sheet show median 165ms, p95 290ms, p99 540ms. so medians improved, p95 similar, p99 higher in our run, likely tail due to cold KV cache events under that traffic pattern.
[00:52] Priya: can you repeat the conditions? iirc we had a ramp to 400 concurrent over 15 minutes with steady state for 30.
[01:00] Ethan: yes that's the load profile. we saw periodic cache misses when new prompt prefixes came in, and a few spikes correlated with background checkpointing on the node — we suspect the q4 quantize background compaction caused a brief latency spike.
[01:20] Tomasz: background checkpointing? that wasn't obvious in your earlier docs, is that something we can disable for the pilot?
[01:28] Ethan: you can — we can pin GC windows and compaction to off hours. we also have K V cache priming scripts that will warm prefixes observed in production traces.
[01:40] Jordan: mm — okay, so the p99 delta vs NimbusServe is about 70ms worse for you in this run, but p50 is better. what's the unit cost delta?
[01:50] Maya: cost per token in this dev run is slightly higher because we were running with fp16 and a conservative batching policy. with quantize-int8 profile and more aggressive batching we estimate unit cost down 18-25% vs run today, and still match or beat NimbusServe while keeping quality within your QA thresholds.
[02:10] Priya: do you have confidence in quality with int8? our regen tests flagged a 2.8% change in rouge on a few prompts last week.
[02:20] Ethan: yeah, that was on a very aggressive profile. we recommend the "balanced int8" profile for now — it trims perf at tail while keeping BLEU/ROUGE drift under 0.7% in our internal tests. we can run an A/B on your prompt set.
[02:36] Ana: from security side, i need to know about KMS and key rotation, also whether logs include PII and retention windows.
[02:44] Lina: we'll share the SOC2 pack and our private deployment spec. Redwood Private supports BYOK via customer-managed KMS and audit logs for inference requests and model actions.
[02:58] Ana: okay please send the docs.
[03:04] Maya: noted. also, we attached the annotated benchmark spreadsheet — link's in the notes — that shows the raw JMeter traces, statistical cleanups and the script we used to generate the requests.
[03:18] Benji: quick question — how much does routing to a cheaper model help during high load?
[03:24] Ethan: good question, Benji. smart routing helps. we can route latency-tolerant endpoints to a cheaper quantized variant and keep the critical endpoints pinned to the high-SLA variant; this reduced overall unit cost by ~30% in a previous pilot.
[03:40] Jordan: so practically, for our billing case we want a routing policy that keeps 95% of traffic on the low-cost path but guarantees the top 20% most latency-sensitive calls hit the low-latency instance.
[03:52] Ethan: yes, we can implement a priority-based policy tied to request tags; we also have an automatic fallback to NimbusServe you can enable for brief capacity exhaustion windows.
[04:06] Priya: how reliable is the fallback? we don't want inconsistency in outputs between providers.
[04:12] Maya: fallback is functionally compatible but you will see output variance between models. we can scaffold a reranking layer to normalize outputs if needed, or do gradual canary to validate equivalence.
[04:28] Jordan: what's the plan for the 24h tail capture?
[04:32] Ethan: i'll kick off the 24h tail run today against the Dedicated dev slot; we'll simulate the same token distribution you sent and capture p50/p95/p99 and node-level traces.
[04:45] Tomasz: please also log kernel-level GPU metrics, memory, and the moment of cache eviction so we can correlate.
[04:52] Ethan: yep, we'll include GPU SMI traces plus our runtime logs.
[04:58] Ana: about compliance - we need proof of encryption at rest and in transit, plus a contact for breach notifications.
[05:06] Lina: i'll route the SOC2 summary and the breach contact card after the call.
[05:12] Maya: great, let's recap the deliverables and next steps...
[05:18] (cross talk)
[05:22] Maya: action items — maya will send the annotated sheet, ethan kicks off tail run, jordan shares real payload distribution, ana shares KMS/retention. schedule follow-up.
[05:34] Jordan: sounds good. thanks team.
[05:36] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with results and propose a canary window. bye.
